beats.headline: Why does your alert fire, but you still can't find the bug?
beats.subline: Monitoring tells you something is broken. Observability tells you why.
beats.narration: Monitoring tells you that your p99 latency is spiking. But when you're staring at a dashboard, you're still blind to the root cause. You need observability to connect the dots.

beats.title: Monitoring vs. Observability
beats.narration: Monitoring is about known unknowns—thresholds you expect to breach. Observability is for the unknown unknowns, letting you query the system's internal state using logs, metrics, and traces.

beats.title: The Triage Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Connecting the three pillars

nodes.label: Loki
nodes.detail: Filter by traceId for root cause

beats.narration: The triage path is simple: fire an alert on metrics, jump to the specific trace via an exemplar, and filter logs by that trace ID to find the exact database lock.

beats.title: Micrometer Observation API

Only for traces. Never put unbounded IDs in metrics or you'll crash Prometheus.

beats.narration: Use the Micrometer Observation API. Distinguish between low-cardinality tags for metrics and high-cardinality tags for traces. Never mix them up, or you'll trigger a cardinality explosion.

beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we look at how to propagate trace context across network hops using the W3C standard.

beats.headline: How do you track a request across 10 microservices?
beats.subline: The W3C TraceContext header is the glue holding your distributed system together.
beats.narration: When a request travels from an API gateway to a Kafka broker and finally a database, how do you keep the context? You need a standard wire format.

beats.title: Tracing Architecture
beats.subtitle: OTLP and Collector decoupling
beats.narration: Don't send traces directly to your backend. Send them to an OpenTelemetry Collector. It decouples your app, scrubs sensitive data, and handles complex tail-based sampling.

beats.title: W3C TraceContext Header
beats.caption: The standard for distributed propagation

lines.text: # 00: version | 4bf9...: trace ID | 00f0...: span ID | 01: flags

beats.narration: The traceparent header is the W3C standard. It carries the trace ID and parent span ID across HTTP and Kafka headers, ensuring downstream services attach to the same span tree.

beats.narration: In Spring Boot 3, just add the micrometer-tracing bridge and the OTLP exporter. This enables automatic instrumentation for REST clients, JDBC, and Kafka.

beats.title: Tracing Part Done
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Head vs Tail-based sampling →
beats.narration: Next, we tackle the cost of tracing—why you should never record 100% of your traffic and how tail-based sampling saves the day.

beats.headline: Recording 100% of traces is a fast way to go bankrupt.
beats.subline: Storage costs for tracing are high. Here is how to sample intelligently.
beats.narration: At 50,000 requests per second, you're generating millions of spans. You don't need all of them. You need the ones that fail or run slow.

beats.title: Sampling Strategies
beats.narration: Head-based sampling is cheap but blind. Tail-based sampling buffers traces in the collector, allowing you to keep every error or slow request while dropping the boring, healthy ones.

beats.title: Tail-Sampling Config
beats.code:
processors:
  tail_sampling:
    policies:
      - name: errors
        type: status_code
        status_code: { status_codes: [ERROR] }
      - name: slow
        type: latency
        latency: { threshold_ms: 1000 }

steps.explanation: Keep every single trace that contains an error.

beats.narration: Configure your OTel collector with tail-sampling policies. This ensures you never miss a production incident, even if it happens rarely.

beats.title: The Load-Balancing Requirement
beats.subtitle: Trace-ID aware routing

nodes.label: Collector Pool
nodes.detail: All spans for traceId land here

beats.narration: Crucial rule: tail-sampling requires that all spans for a single trace ID land on the same collector instance. Use a load balancer to hash by trace ID.

beats.title: Sampling Strategy Set
takeaways: Hash spans by traceId for consistency

beats.narration: Finally, in Part 4, we fix your logs. We'll cover structured JSON logging and how to prevent context leaks in your thread pools.

beats.headline: Are your logs still just plain text?
beats.subline: If you aren't using structured JSON, you're making your on-call engineer's life miserable.
beats.narration: Parsing plain text logs with regex is a nightmare. Structured JSON makes your logs instantly searchable and indexable.

beats.title: MDC Context Propagation

steps.explanation: Mapped Diagnostic Context attaches data to all logs in this thread.
Use try-with-resources to prevent thread-local leaks.

beats.narration: MDC is your best friend. It attaches business IDs to every log line. But watch out—if you don't clear it, the next request on that thread will inherit stale data.

beats.title: ELK vs. Loki
beats.narration: Choose ELK if you need full-text search across weeks of data. Choose Loki if you want to save money and keep your logs close to your metrics and traces in Grafana.

beats.title: Async Context Propagation

steps.explanation: Propagates MDC and trace context across thread boundaries.

beats.narration: When using async threads, context is lost. Use the ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator in your executor config to ensure your trace IDs follow your code across threads.
